name: Burnt coconut shell tooth blacking

card.summary: A traditional dye in which burnt coconut shell is used to blacken teeth, a beauty custom in parts of Southeast Asia that gives a glossy dark finish.
card.aka: tooth blackening, teeth lacquering, nhuom rang (Vietnam)
card.note: Historical cultural practice; dental and medical sources describe it mainly as a custom, not a modern cosmetic treatment.

quick.overview:
Tooth blackening is the custom of dyeing teeth black, practised historically across Southeast Asia, Oceania, Japan and parts of India. In Vietnam one of the materials used was burnt coconut shell, applied as a dye solution to produce a dark, lacquer-like surface.

In the cultures that did it, dark teeth were regarded as beautiful and a sign of maturity. Its appearance payoff was cultural: a uniform black finish that was the standard of beauty rather than a flaw.
quick.how: Descriptions of the Vietnamese practice say teeth were first cleaned with materials such as betel, charcoal powder and salt, then treated with preparation liquids before dye solutions were applied; burnt coconut shell, an iron solution and other substances are listed among the dyes. It was typically done around puberty and could be repeated.
quick.risks: Accounts describe the process as sometimes painful and as causing swollen gums. Historical writers claimed the dye preserved teeth, but these are traditional accounts. Practice has declined strongly since the early twentieth century.

lead: Burnt coconut shell is one of the materials recorded in the Vietnamese form of tooth blackening, a beauty custom in which teeth were dyed black. Tooth blackening was common across Southeast Asian and Oceanic cultures and was also practised in Japan before the Meiji era and in parts of India.[1]

In Vietnam the custom (nhuom rang) was widespread among the Kinh majority and many minority groups into the early twentieth century. Dyes listed in descriptions include burnt coconut shell, an iron solution and, in one nineteenth-century text, a red ant paste followed by black alum.[1]
For those who practised it, the darkened teeth were the beauty ideal and a mark of adulthood and refinement. No clinical trials of coconut-shell dye have been published.

angle.text: The dye changes tooth colour to a uniform black. In the cultures that practised it, this was the intended attractive look, usually adopted around puberty.

infobox: Vietnam; wider Southeast Asian blackening tradition
Largely faded since the early 20th century

paras: Tooth blackening, also called teeth lacquering, covers several regional recipes. Japanese ohaguro used ferric acetate and plant tannins, South Asian missi used iron and copper salts with tannin-rich plants, and the Vietnamese tradition included burnt coconut shell among its dye solutions.[1]

Archaeological evidence in Vietnam dates to about 400 BCE, and colonial reports in the 1930s claimed that most Tonkinese farmers had darkened teeth. The custom declined through the twentieth century under French and Western influence.[1] Blackening was tied to the transition to adulthood and to ideas of beauty and civilisation.[1]

Descriptions say the process could be painful and cause swollen gums, and are careful to distinguish blackening from the stained teeth of betel chewing. A sixteenth-century writer claimed the dye kept teeth sound into old age; this is a historical account.[1]
